text:
The chair had been set out with the rubbish on Tuesday, though collection wasn’t due until Thursday. It stood beneath the plane tree at Bleecker and Morton, its legs uneven on the pavement, its upholstered back blackened by something that looked less like fire than a long, private argument. A strip of green fabric remained along the seat’s edge. When the wind lifted it, the strip fluttered like a flag flown by a defeated country.

I noticed it while waiting for a bus that had already stopped running. The city had been warning us about rain for days, in the calm language it used for things it couldn’t prevent. By six, clouds hung low over the rooftops, and the streetlights came on with the tentative look of guests arriving too early.

The couple appeared at the far end of the block.

They were neither young nor old enough to attract attention. The man wore a brown overcoat and carried a paper bag folded neatly at the top. The woman wore an unbuttoned navy raincoat and had a small, pale face arranged for someone else’s comfort. They walked close together without touching. He spoke; she listened. At the corner he glanced at her, and she smiled—not broadly, but with the economical movement of someone opening a door.

It was the smile that held me. There was nothing remarkable in it. I had seen such smiles at dinner parties, in elevators, on trains when one person shifted to make room for another. But this one seemed to belong less to the woman than to the space around her. The rain softened. The traffic briefly grew quiet.

They passed the chair. The woman looked at it.

The man kept walking. She followed, but turned her head once more, as if expecting the chair to say something.

I began after them.

I can’t tell you why. A person can spend years in a city learning to disregard the people who interest them most. I had no good reason to follow, and several not to: rain was coming, I had groceries at home, and following strangers sounds sinister when described aloud.

They walked north, then west, through wet streets with the uncertainty of people who had made the same journey many times and still disagreed about the route. At Hudson Street, the woman looked back. I ducked into a doorway. When I looked again, she had turned away, and the man had taken her arm with the absent-minded firmness of someone steadying a chair.

They entered a narrow brick house with little gardens behind iron railings. A light glowed in a second-floor window. I walked to the next corner, doubled back, and stood beneath the awning of a closed florist.

Upstairs, the couple moved in and out of sight. The man took off his coat and hung it over a chair. The woman stood by the window, seeming to look into the street. I couldn’t tell whether her gaze passed over me or through me. Then the curtain came down.

The rain began in earnest. Water ran along the curb in a silver stream. I should have gone home. Instead, I watched the house.

There is a point at which a watcher begins inventing a life for the watched. First the inventions are practical: they must have a kitchen, pay rent, own a kettle. Then they grow tender, and then strange. I imagined the man had once been cheerful and the woman never had. I imagined they had met at a funeral or in a doctor’s waiting room. The paper bag, which had sagged as if it held books, became full of pears.

The water reached the curb, then covered it. At ten, a taxi stalled in the intersection. Its driver rolled up his trousers and walked away with the stiff dignity of a man leaving a ship.

I thought again of the chair: the green strip, the blackened back, the woman’s second look.

The flood rose by inches, then seemed to rise all at once. It carried leaves and cigarette packs, then a plastic crate and an orange construction cone. The house stood on slightly higher ground, but the water reached its stoop. The first-floor windows were dark.

At eleven-thirty, a light came on upstairs.

The woman crossed the room and stopped beside the window. She wore a pale blouse now, her hair gathered at her neck. Behind her, the man sat at a table, head lowered, hands spread flat before him.

Then she turned and sat in a chair.

I knew it at once, though it was impossible. It wasn’t the burned chair from the corner. This one had a wooden frame and a faded red cushion, an ordinary apartment chair worn into the room’s understanding of itself. She sat with her back to the window and rested her hands on the arms.

I looked down the street. The flood had lifted something from the corner and sent it turning toward me. Beneath a streetlamp I saw the blackened back of the chair, its green strip streaming behind it. It had come loose from the rubbish and was floating toward the house.

The woman turned her head.

She couldn’t have seen the chair; it was still half a block away. Yet she rose and went to the window. The man remained at the table. She watched the chair drift down the street, as if it had been invited.

It struck the iron railing, turned, bumped the gate, and settled against it. For a moment it seemed to be trying the entrance.

The woman pressed one hand to the glass.

The rain had stopped, but the water continued to climb. The chair lifted from the railing and moved on with the current. As it passed beneath her window, she followed it with her eyes, her hand still against the glass.

Then the room went dark.

From inside the house came a sound—not quite a crash, more like the falling of something that had been standing for a long time.

I stayed until the water reached my shoes, then left. I didn’t see the couple again. The next day, people carried wet mattresses to the curb and turned their hands palm-up toward the sky. The house showed no visible damage. Its windows were closed, its gate intact.

The chair was gone.

A week later I passed the corner again. The plane tree had dropped most of its leaves. Someone had left a new chair beneath it, upholstered in green, its back intact and its legs even. I stood beside it longer than I meant to.

A woman came along the sidewalk, walking alone. She paused and looked at the chair.

She smiled.

It was an ordinary, small, polite smile, meant for no one in particular. Still, I looked for the man beside her, the brown coat, the paper bag. Down the block there was only wet pavement, shining faintly in the late afternoon.
